title_eng: Reply to ‘Comment on Photoplethysmography sampling frequency: pilot assessment of how low can we go to analyze pulse rate variability with reliability?’
abstract:
In his Comment, Hejjel argued that some contents previously published by 
us were inappropriate for the statistical analysis of pulse rate variability due 
to high inter-individual dispersion. He also claimed that data collection over 
5 min for short-term HRV analysis and data collection for an abnormal range 
of people were required. In order to give our perspective on these issues, we 
will discuss and clarify some of the existing literature and our own work 
on this subject, underlining the difference between electrocardiogram and 
photoplethysmogram.

Abstract
In his Comment, Hejjel argued that some contents previously published by 
us were inappropriate for the statistical analysis of pulse rate variability due 
to high inter-individual dispersion. He also claimed that data collection over 
5 min for short-term HRV analysis and data collection for an abnormal range 
of people were required. In order to give our perspective on these issues, we 
will discuss and clarify some of the existing literature and our own work 
on this subject, underlining the difference between electrocardiogram and 
photoplethysmogram.
Keywords: electrocardiogram, heart rate variability, photoplethysmography, 
pulse rate variability
(Some figures may appear in colour only in the online journal)
1. Overall reply
Hejjel raised three issues about our paper (Choi and Shin 2017) in his ‘Comment on: 
Photoplethysmography sampling frequency: pilot assessment of how low can we go to ana-
lyze pulse rate variability with reliability?’ The issues raised could be summarized as follows: 
(1) statistical validation under inherently high inter-individual dispersion of heart rate vari-
ability (HRV) parameters; (2) the need for further studies in people with decreased HRV; and 
(3) the need for further investigation on the recording time of electrocardiogram (ECG). In

the characteristics of the data that we collected. In the second part of this Reply, we present a 
point-by-point response to these issues raised by Hejjel.
First, we want to clarify that the main topic of our research was to investigate the effect of 
sampling frequency on pulse rate variability (PRV) based on photoplethysmography (PPG) 
for a person without a disease. In terms of PRV , whether PRV is an effective surrogate method 
of HRV remains controversial. Several studies have evaluated PRV as a surrogate for HRV 
(Veerman et al 1994, Laude et al 1995, Mueck-Weymann et al 2002, Lu et al 2008). These 
studies showed that the physical position of a subject could cause divergence in PRV from 
HRV . This is because PRV is tightly coupled with mechanical phenomena such as respiration 
and thoracic vascular systems activity. These activities have more influence at a standing posi-
tion than at a supine position (Saul et al 1991). Mental condition is another factor that may 
cause divergence in PRV from HRV . Previous studies have shown that mental stress can lead 
to increased pulse wave velocity (PWV) (Lydakis et al 2008), and a change in PWV could 
induce variations not only in pulse transit time (PTT) but also in PRV . These research studies 
suggest that PRV is the most acceptable surrogate of HRV . However, it is only recommended 
at resting condition. Although HRV and PRV are very similar, they can have different values 
depending on their application. Much research is currently ongoing to determine the reason 
why. However, in Hejjel’s Comment, he did not consider the differences between PRV and 
HRV . Thus, it is necessary to consider the specificity of PRV .
Our study hypothesized that HRV and PRV could vary with sampling frequency due to dif-
ferences in signal characteristics. ECG is the sum of electrical activity that occurs throughout 
the heart, whereas PPG reflects blood volume changes caused by mechanical cardiac contrac-
tion and vessel movement. The spatiotemporal characteristics of these signals are different.
In frequency domain analysis of PRV , the frequency range of clinical ECG is well-known to 
be 0.05–100 Hz. Most of the power of the QRS complex is concentrated at 17 Hz (Tompkins 
1993). However, most of the power of PPG is known to be concentrated at less than 10 Hz, 
consisting of a standing wave related to the pulsatile component and harmonics (Shin et al 
2009). Figure 1 represents an example of the power spectrum of ECG and PPG that we col-
lected in this paper. As mentioned above, the power of the PPG was concentrated at a low

frequency (under 10 Hz), whereas the power of the ECG spread uniformly to a relatively high 
frequency range.
In the time domain analysis of PRV , considering that random noise in the range of fs/2 is 
generated at sampling frequency fs, the PRV of the PPG signal when the frequency power is 
concentrated relatively low is more robust to low frequency sampling compared to the HRV 
of the ECG signal. Figure 2 shows variations of ECG and PPG signals in more detail accord-
ing to sampling rate in the time domain. Generally, a healthy subject’s ECG waveform has 
a sharp shape, with various waves such as P, QRS, T-wave, and QRS complex. However, the 
PPG waveform is relatively simple and round-shaped compared with ECG because it comes 
from the blood pressure waveform. Comparing waveforms in the frequency domain, the QRS 
complex of the ECG has a relatively sharp shape in high frequency, whereas the PPG wave-
form has a round shape in low frequency. Therefore, by applying down-sampling, the ECG 
waveform is more distorted than the PPG waveform because the frequency of ECG is higher 
than that of PPG. In addition, the T-wave of the ECG could be confused with the QRS at a 
lower sampling frequency of the ECG. In conclusion, HRV and PRV are similar to each other 
in explaining heart rate variability. However, they have different patterns in down sampling 
due to differences in the signal shape in the time domain and signal power in the frequency 
domain.
